source.title: The Languini Kitchen: Enabling Language Modelling Research at Different Scales of Compute
source.authors: Aleksandar Stanic; Dylan R. Ashley; O. Serikov; Louis Kirsch; Francesco Faccio; J. Schmidhuber; Thomas Hofmann; Imanol Schlag

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out language-model performance across compute classes and fits scaling trends, but uses a different dataset, compute protocol, and normalized perplexity measure from the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper measures normalized perplexity (cross-entropy per byte transformed by exponentiation) on held-out books and reports best runs across 6–96 accelerator hours for GPT and qLSTM models. The evidence covers compute scaling, not independent validation of predictions on much larger runs. It does not test parameter- or token-scaling laws, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture shape at fixed parameter count, other modalities or training regimes, or downstream-task predictability. It discusses cited scaling-law work and cites external results; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its compute-optimal batch-size analysis is not a test of the claim's parameter/token allocation version.
record.test_reason: It trains GPT and qLSTM language models from scratch at five compute classes (6–96 RTX-3090 hours). It fits power laws to the held-out normalised perplexity of the best run per class, against both accelerator time and FLOPs. This is a different protocol aimed at the compute-scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that GPT has better perplexity at all compute classes up to 96 h. The qLSTM shows a steeper, predictable scaling law because it needs fewer tokens, so extrapolation gives a crossover at ~50,000 accelerator hours. In FLOPs, qLSTM already beats GPT after ~2 exaFLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses best-run comparisons by accelerator-hour compute class and normalized perplexity per byte, rather than the original studies' scaling setups; compares GPT and qLSTM on the Languini Books benchmark.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family changes the fitted slope: the reported qLSTM slopes are steeper than GPT slopes. The selected model configuration, batch size, and token count also vary by compute class.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted compute-scaling exponents differ by architecture: qLSTM is steeper than GPT on both axes. The authors call scaling laws model-specific.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-scaling exponents of LM loss are architecture-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: Compute-optimal batch size is roughly 256–512 across GPT sizes and rises slightly with longer training (Figure 8). It is much smaller for qLSTM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal batch size depends weakly on model size and is model-specific.

record.problems: Only five compute classes spanning 6–96 hours are reported. Fits use the best selected run/configuration at each class, and model configurations vary across classes. No uncertainty estimates or direct validation of extrapolated large-run predictions are reported.

untested.parts: Only about 1.2 orders of magnitude of compute (6–96 h; 0.24–11.9 exaFLOPs) are covered, not several. Parameter and token scaling are not separately varied with the other factors non-bottlenecked. The measure is normalised perplexity per byte, not raw loss.
The fits are extrapolated to ~50,000 h, but no larger run checks the prediction.
No fitted law for loss-optimal parameters or tokens vs compute. Best config per class grows (GPT small to medium; qLSTM mini to small), but this is not fitted.
Shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested.
Data, schedule and fitting method are not varied.

missing.what: Normalised perplexity on 5 out-of-distribution book splits for best GPT and qLSTM at each compute class. It decreases monotonically with compute in all splits, and regression lines are shown.
Statement that qLSTM beats GPT after roughly 2 exaFLOPs on the FLOPs axis.

record.verdict_notes: Each fit uses only five best-config points, with no uncertainty reported, and the config changes across classes. The power law is stated for normalised perplexity (exp of loss per byte). Over this narrow range that is near-equivalent to a power law in loss, but not identical. The authors are not original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compute scaling only, using normalized perplexity on held-out books over 6–96 accelerator hours. It does not independently vary parameters or tokens while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecked, and does not establish the trend across several orders of magnitude.
The paper extrapolates fitted trends to an intersection near 50,000 accelerator hours, but does not test those predictions against observed runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not estimate how loss-minimizing parameter and token counts grow with a fixed compute budget. Its batch-size analysis is not this allocation question.
GPT and qLSTM are compared at roughly similar parameter/FLOP scales, but depth, width, and other architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
No other modalities, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws are tested.
The paper focuses on held-out perplexity and does not test downstream-task performance or its predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study reports different fitted scaling slopes for GPT and qLSTM, supporting model-specific trends. It does not systematically vary parameter counting, data, training schedule, or fitting method, test whether published laws disagree, or report curves bending away from a single power law.

source_check.reason: The fitted metric is normalized perplexity, defined as exp(L/B), rather than loss. A power law in this transformed metric does not establish V1's power-law loss; the measured compute range also does not span several orders of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Choice of compute measure (accelerator time vs FLOPs), qLSTM vs GPT
relationships.reason: The qLSTM exponent shifts from −0.112 to −0.134 with the x-axis choice (GPT only −0.082 to −0.084). The GPT/qLSTM crossover moves from ~2 exaFLOPs to ~50,000 h (r11–r14).
relationships.display_finding: Changing the compute measure shifts the qLSTM exponent from −0.112 to −0.134 and GPT's from −0.082 to −0.084, while their crossover changes from approximately 2 exaFLOPs to approximately 50,000 hours.
